response.title: Bringing the School Wetland Back to Life
response.passage: On the first day of the project, students noticed that several young plants around the school pond were fragile, with thin stems that bent easily in the wind. Their biology teacher explained that the pond was a habitat for frogs and insects, so even small changes could affect local wildlife. To conserve water, the class placed a rain barrel beside the greenhouse and used its collected rain to water the plants. However, after weeks without rain, water in the pond became scarce, and the muddy edge began to crack. Each Friday, student pairs monitor the pond’s water level and count the frogs they can see. To keep their records dependable, they use a reliable measuring stick and check the water at the same spot each time. The class also removed plastic litter and planted native reeds, hoping these steps would restore the pond over time. After six weeks, the students compared their notes with the first week’s results. They found more frogs near the new reeds and a higher water level after the rain. These changes were evidence that the project was helping the pond recover.

response.title: A Garden That Teaches
response.passage:
Our school science club started a small garden beside the gym. We wanted to learn why some plants grew well while others did not. Every Wednesday, we go to the garden before class and check the leaves and soil. Each student can take a small jar of soil back to the science room. There, we compare samples from sunny and shady spots, using the same amount of water for each plant.

Our teacher suggested that we carry out a simple test for the first time this term. We will place two similar seedlings in different amounts of sunlight and record their growth in a table. Mina is especially interested in how light changes the color of leaves, so she has offered to keep the records. During the summer break, two club members will look after the seedlings. They will water them on schedule and tell the teacher if any leaves begin to turn yellow. By sharing the work and writing down what we see, we hope to understand the garden better and make it healthier.

response.title: Reading the River
response.passage:
On a warm Saturday in July, the Green Club met beside a river that ran through the town park. Heavy rain had washed plastic cups and branches onto the bank, and the mess was beginning to bother visitors. The club had only a few pairs of gloves and one coil of rope. Its members first thought they could finish the cleanup by themselves. The students agreed to cooperate with the park staff, since neither group could clear the bank alone. That decision gave them enough people to divide the work safely.

Before anyone entered the shallow water, Ms. Lin asked the group to study the river from the path. A map showed that the stream bent sharply near a footbridge, and one student guessed that the turn might explain why so much litter had collected there. To check that guess, two students chose to observe the water for ten minutes and mark where floating leaves slowed down. Their notes showed that leaves gathered just below the bend, where the bank was wide and easy to reach. The team decided to begin there instead of spreading out along the whole river.

Near the footbridge, a volunteer noticed that the rope in their kit had a frayed section. Ms. Lin went to the park shed and brought back a reliable rope that she had checked earlier that morning. With that secure line in place, the students could pull larger branches toward the bank without stepping into deeper water. They filled several bags with cups and wrappers, while the staff moved heavy branches out of the walking path. No one rushed, and the group paused whenever a task required more hands.

By midday, the bank looked much cleaner, but a few bottles remained caught among the reeds. A strong current kept pushing them farther downstream whenever someone reached toward them from the shore. The team left those bottles alone and reported their location to the park workers, who had a long-handled tool for the job. Before leaving, the students checked the path for loose gloves and thanked the staff for their help. The club planned to return after the next heavy rain, now knowing where litter was most likely to collect.
removals: The students agreed to cooperate with the park staff, since neither group could clear the bank alone.

response.title: A Fair for Every Reader
response.passage:
Our school library held a book fair in the gym to raise money for new reading lamps. Students brought gently used books from home, and the library staff checked each one for torn pages or missing covers. On Thursday, the helpers arranged the books by age group so visitors could find stories that suited them. Several younger classes had asked to visit, so the organizers set aside a small selection for them. For next week's reading visit, the club decided to reserve six storybooks in a separate box. A bright label on that box helped the teachers find the books when their classes arrived.

The fair opened on Friday afternoon, just after the last class ended. The timetable was posted beside the gym doors, and every class had a short visit before students could shop freely. The current schedule gives each class only fifteen minutes at the display. Because it was so tight, the student guides prepared a quick tour and pointed visitors toward the right shelves. This plan helped the younger students choose books without making the line grow too long.

By noon, a shortage of helpers had become clear at the busiest table. To cover it, two students left the checkout desk and took turns answering questions there. A teacher watched the desk while they were away, so buyers could still pay without waiting too long. Meanwhile, another group wrote down the names of books that sold out, giving the librarian a clear list for future orders. Although the gym became noisy, the helpers kept the aisles open and reminded visitors to carry books carefully.

When the fair ended, the students counted the money and returned the unsold books to the library. They also checked the gym floor for price tags and paper scraps before leaving. The librarian compared the sales list with the books still on the shelves. That comparison showed which kinds of stories had attracted the most interest. The school used the results to choose new titles, and the students felt proud that their careful work would help more classmates enjoy reading.
removals: For next week's reading visit, the club decided to reserve six storybooks in a separate box.
The current schedule gives each class only fifteen minutes at the display.

The librarian compared the sales list with the books still on the shelves.

response.title: Reading a Creek Together
response.passage:
In early spring, a high school science class began checking a small creek behind the town library. After heavy rain, the water often looked brown, and neighbors wondered whether litter or soil was affecting insects and fish. The students could not test every part of the creek, so they chose a stretch beside a footbridge, where stones formed a shallow pool before the water passed under the road. They marked three observation points with orange flags and drew their locations on a map. Before taking samples, they would observe each point for five minutes, using the same routine at every flag. On the first visit, this routine helped everyone notice details that might otherwise have been missed, such as foam caught between two rocks.

One pair measured the water’s clarity and temperature, while another sketched litter and plant growth along the bank. The numbers showed where the water was murkiest, but the sketches showed that fallen leaves had collected near those spots. Because neither numbers nor sketches alone could explain why conditions changed, the two teams had to cooperate. When they placed their notes side by side, they saw that the shallow pool trapped leaves after rain, which made the water look darker without proving that it was unsafe.

To compare samples fairly, the teacher brought a small electronic sensor and showed the class how to clean it between tests. At first, its readings jumped from one test to the next, so the students checked its battery and rinsed the sensor again. After Ms. Lin replaced its weak battery and tested it three times, it gave reliable readings. That consistency allowed the class to compare results from later visits with more confidence, though they still treated one measurement as only part of the story.

The students also wanted to understand how quickly water moved through the stretch. They placed a light leaf upstream of a marked section and set a net near the bend. The current carried each leaf toward the bend, where the volunteers could catch it safely. By timing each trip between the marks, they could compare the creek’s flow on rainy and dry days. At the end of the month, the class shared its chart with neighbors and explained both what the observations suggested and what they could not establish. Their careful work gave the town a useful starting point for future checks, rather than a quick answer based on appearance alone.
removals: Before taking samples, they would observe each point for five minutes, using the same routine at every flag.
Because neither numbers nor sketches alone could explain why conditions changed, the two teams had to cooperate.
After Ms. Lin replaced its weak battery and tested it three times, it gave reliable readings.
The current carried each leaf toward the bend, where the volunteers could catch it safely.
response.extraOption: Since no one could reach the creek, the students completed every test inside the library.

response.title: A Garden That Could Wait
response.passage:
At Oak Hill High, the science club cared for a small garden beside the cafeteria. Students watered it from an outdoor tap, but they noticed that the tap sometimes ran weakly after several dry days. The garden’s new seedlings needed steady care, and the club wanted a way to keep them alive without using as much tap water. This shortage had become especially clear during the previous month’s dry week, when the garden beds began to crack. The head custodian explained that the school could collect rainwater, but only if the students stored it safely and followed the school’s rules.

The club made a plan before the next storm. One group measured the roof area and estimated how much rain the gutters might collect, while another checked which containers had tight lids. They also decided to reserve two covered containers for seedlings they would plant later in the term. The containers would stay empty until the garden’s next planting day, so the club could keep its promise without taking water away from the plants that already needed it. Students then asked the principal to confirm the school’s policy before they set anything up.

The current school rule allowed collected rainwater to be used on plants, but not for washing tools or filling bottles. That limit meant the club had to keep the storage area separate from the drinking fountains and label each container clearly. The custodian helped them connect a clean barrel to one downspout and showed them how to check its lid after windy weather. After the first storm, the students measured the water and recorded the date, rainfall, and amount collected. They used some of it on the garden and left the two reserved containers untouched.

For several weeks, the club compared its records with the weather and the garden’s condition. On dry days, the stored water kept the older plants from wilting, while the reserved supply remained ready for the later seedlings. The students did not claim that one barrel could solve every water problem at school. Instead, their dated chart showed how much rain the roof could provide and when the garden needed it most. At the end of the term, they shared the results with the principal and suggested adding a second barrel if the school approved the cost. Their small project gave the next group of students a clear plan to build on.
removals: This shortage had become especially clear during the previous month’s dry week, when the garden beds began to crack.
They also decided to reserve two covered containers for seedlings they would plant later in the term.
The current school rule allowed collected rainwater to be used on plants, but not for washing tools or filling bottles.
Instead, their dated chart showed how much rain the roof could provide and when the garden needed it most.

response.title: A Closer Look at Willow Creek
response.passage:
After heavy rain, students at a local high school visited Willow Creek to learn how weather changes a stream. Their science teacher asked them to measure the water at three marked places and note what they saw. The class worked in small groups. Some students held the measuring sticks, while others wrote down the results, so they had to cooperate to finish the survey before lunch.

At the first place, the water looked calm. Farther downstream, it moved quickly around a bend. The students wanted to know whether the water also moved faster near the middle of the stream. They placed small paper boats at the bank and in the center, then watched carefully. The boats in the center traveled farther in the same amount of time. The students recorded the direction and distance rather than guessing from how the water looked.

To make their notes reliable, two students read each measurement aloud while a partner checked it against the marks on the stick. If they disagreed, they measured again and wrote down the new result. Their teacher reminded them that one careful check was more useful than several rushed guesses. The class also kept a copy of the notes at school, so they would still have the results if a page got wet during the trip.

Back in class, the groups compared their records. They found that the center water carried the boats downstream faster than the water near the bank. The teacher asked them to repeat the survey on a dry day. The students planned to compare the results and see whether the stream changed after the rain.

response.title: A Sensor Plan for the Greenhouse
response.passage:
The environmental club at Harbor High planned to use temperature sensors in every bed of its greenhouse before the school science fair. The sensors would help students notice which plants needed extra care. However, several devices stopped working, and the replacement boards had not arrived. Because of the shortage, the club had only six working sensors for ten beds.

Rather than place them wherever they happened to fit, the students checked the greenhouse map and talked with the science teacher. Four beds already held young plants that needed close attention. The other beds would receive seedlings the following week. The club decided to put four sensors beside the young plants and reserve the other two in a cabinet until the new seedlings arrived. That way, the team could use all six devices when they would be most helpful.

The club wrote down its current plan on a board near the greenhouse door: check the four active sensors each morning, keep two in the cabinet, and move them when the seedlings arrive. The teacher explained that the plan could change if the replacement boards came early. The students agreed to update the board if that happened, so everyone would know which devices were in use.

On Monday, the students followed the plan and recorded the readings before class. They found that one bed was warmer than the others, so they opened its window for a short time. The club could not yet monitor every bed, but its notes showed that the limited sensors were being used where they could guide an immediate decision.

distractors: They placed all six sensors beside the young plants right away.

response.title: Reading a Stream Together
response.passage:
When students at Brookfield High began checking a stream near their town, they hoped to give the community useful information, not to prove that the water was either clean or dirty. Four students cooperated with a park worker and two nearby residents. They agreed to visit the same three points on two different days and to record what they saw before discussing what it might mean.

On their first visit, the students arrived the morning after heavy rain. Near the bridge, a fallen leaf traveled quickly past a stone at the water’s edge. The park worker explained that rain upstream can change the flow even when the sky above the stream is clear. The students also observed the water’s color, but their teacher reminded them that clear water alone could not show whether it was safe. They collected samples and wrote down the time and location for each one.

The group used the same thermometer at every point. At the first stop, however, one student left it in direct sunlight while writing notes. Its reading was higher than the next two readings. Rather than choosing the result they liked best, the students moved the thermometer into the shade and measured again. The new reading matched the other two. Their teacher said that a reliable record depended on careful, repeated measurements, not on a single number.

A week later, after several dry days, the team returned. The water’s surface looked almost still, but a leaf placed beside the same stone moved steadily downstream. The current was slower than it had been after the rain, yet it had not stopped. This time, the students took longer to finish because they checked each other’s notes and compared the same locations. In their report, they described the two visits separately and explained that the different weather might have affected what they observed. They did not claim that the stream had become safer or more polluted. Instead, they recommended more visits before drawing a firm conclusion. The park worker added that the students’ careful record would help decide where to focus future checks.

distractors: The students tried to prove that the stream was unsafe after the rain.

response.title: A Careful Plan for Saturday Meals
response.passage:
When the Eastside Community Center began serving free Saturday lunches, the student volunteers expected about thirty-five guests each week. By early winter, the sign-up list had grown to more than fifty names. The center had enough food for the next lunch, but its delivery of canned goods might arrive late. At the same time, three volunteers had stopped coming because of schedule conflicts. Coordinator Ms. Lin wanted the program to keep serving families without making promises the team could not keep.

The volunteers reviewed the menu and the food in storage. They decided to serve soup, rice, and fruit, rather than offer the extra dessert they had discussed. They also chose to reserve twelve cans of fruit for the following Saturday. The supplier had not canceled the order, but could not confirm its arrival date. Ms. Lin explained that saving some food for later would give the team another option if the delivery was delayed.

A few students worried that a shorter menu might disappoint guests. To understand what people needed, they observed the lunch line and asked guests to mark a simple card: Was the meal enough, and which item mattered most? Most guests said the meal was filling. Several wrote that fruit was especially useful because they could take it home. The team added fruit to the next menu, but kept the dessert off it. The answers showed what mattered to guests, while the smaller menu left fewer tasks for the remaining volunteers.

The center’s current plan is to continue the shorter menu for four weeks, keep a small supply in reserve, and track both attendance and deliveries. After that, the volunteers will review their notes before deciding whether to add another dish. Ms. Lin said the plan was temporary, but she did not promise that the menu would grow. The students agreed that a steady lunch each week would help more than a larger meal that the team might not be able to prepare.

items.answer: The delivery date was uncertain, so the team kept some fruit for the following Saturday.
distractors: The supplier canceled the order, so the team used all the fruit at once.
Guests rejected fruit, so the team saved it to replace the soup.
The volunteers had extra time, so the team stored fruit for a special dessert.
